title: Rabbah Taken and the Giants of Gath Fall
summary: In the spring Joab leads the army against Ammon and captures Rabbah while David stays in Jerusalem; David takes the Ammonite king's heavy gold crown and puts the people to forced labor. Then three short battle reports tell how David's warriors killed three descendants of the Rephaim among the Philistines, including a brother of Goliath and a man with six fingers and six toes.
story: The war with Ammon that began in chapter 19 ends here. The chapter then gathers three brief episodes from wars with the Philistines, closing the long section on David's victories that began in chapter 18. What the chapter leaves out is as important as what it includes. Verse 1 says David remained in Jerusalem while Joab besieged Rabbah; in 2 Samuel 11 those same words open the story of David, Bathsheba, and Uriah. The Chronicler moves directly from the siege to its end, and he also omits the rebellions of Absalom and Sheba that fill 2 Samuel 13-20. His purpose is to show David as the king who completed Israel's security and prepared for the temple, which the next chapters take up.
historical:
The chapter draws on three parts of 2 Samuel: the siege of Rabbah in 2 Samuel 11:1, its capture in 12:26-31, and the Philistine battles in 21:18-22. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, stood on the site of modern Amman, Jordan. In 2 Samuel 12:27-29 Joab takes the city's water supply and then summons David to finish the capture so that the victory will bear David's name; Chronicles compresses this.

The Philistine episodes are undated and may come from different points in David's reign. Gezer and Gath were Philistine or border cities, and Gath was the home of Goliath, whom David had killed years before (1 Samuel 17). The Rephaim, or descendants of Rapha, were remembered in Israelite tradition as a people of great stature who lived in Canaan and Transjordan before Israel (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20-21; 3:11). Scholars differ on whether the term names an ethnic group, a clan of warriors, or a legendary category of giants; the text treats these men as formidable opponents who fell to ordinary Israelite soldiers.
cultural:
Spring, after the winter rains, was the normal season for campaigns: roads were passable, and armies could live off the land as crops ripened. The crown weighing a talent of gold, commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms, would have been too heavy to wear for long, and many scholars suggest it was ceremonial or belonged to an idol. The Hebrew for their king, malkam, can also be read as Milcom, the name of the Ammonite god, and some translations take the crown to be his. Placing a defeated king's crown on the victor's head was a public sign of transferred rule.

Verse 3 is difficult. The Hebrew verb here can be read as sawed, and older translations such as the King James Version said David cut the people with saws. The parallel in 2 Samuel 12:31 uses a verb meaning to set or put, and most modern translations read both passages as forced labor with saws, iron picks, and axes, a common fate for conquered populations who were put to work on royal building projects. Polydactyly, extra fingers and toes, is a known human condition; here it is noted as part of what made the Gittite warrior remarkable.
literary: The chapter has two uneven parts: the end of the Ammonite war (verses 1-3) and a small collection of giant-killer stories (verses 4-8). The three stories share a formula: war with the Philistines, a named Israelite, a named descendant of Rapha, and his death. The summary in verse 8 says these fell at the hands of David and his servants. The pattern is quietly significant. Years before, a young David killed Goliath with God's help; now ordinary soldiers of his army do the same. The kind of courage David once showed has spread through his people.

outline.t: David takes the crown and the people are put to labor
Jonathan kills the six-fingered giant at Gath

doctrines.note: Formidable enemies fall to ordinary men. The chapter reinforces the promise of 17:10 that God would subdue David's enemies, and it shows that promise worked out through many people, not David alone.

The Chronicler's selectivity reminds readers that biblical history is written with a purpose. He assumes his readers know Samuel and Kings, and he tells the story so as to highlight God's promise and the temple, without denying what he omits.

words.note: Rapha, the ancestor or eponym of the Rephaim. In verses 6 and 8 these warriors are called descendants of Rapha. The related plural in verse 4 (Rephaim) is used elsewhere both for giant peoples of the past and, in poetic texts, for the shades of the dead.

Charaph, to taunt or defy. The six-fingered giant taunted Israel (verse 7), the same verb used of Goliath defying the armies of the living God in 1 Samuel 17. To taunt Israel was to taunt Israel's God, and in both stories the taunter falls.

Shachat, to ruin or destroy, rendered ravaged in verse 1. The verb describes thorough devastation, and the same verb describes the angel destroying Jerusalem in the next chapter (21:15). Here it describes Joab's campaign against Ammon's land.

christ: The giant-killing stories recall David and Goliath, the story in which the anointed king fights for a people who cannot fight for themselves. Here the victory spreads to David's servants. The New Testament uses a similar pattern for Christ and his people: Christ defeats the powers (Colossians 2:15), and his followers share in that victory, as Paul says in Romans 8:37 that believers are more than conquerors through him. The link is thematic, a pattern of a champion whose victory is shared, rather than a prediction in the text.

hard.q: Who killed Goliath: David, or Elhanan? And why does Chronicles leave out David's sin with Bathsheba?
hard.a:
In 1 Samuel 17 David kills Goliath of Gath. In 2 Samuel 21:19 the Hebrew says Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite killed Goliath the Gittite, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. Some scholars think 2 Samuel 21:19 preserves an older tradition and that the Chronicler harmonized it. Others think the Samuel text has suffered a copying error: in Hebrew, the word for Bethlehemite (bet hallahmi) closely resembles Lahmi, and the word oregim (weavers) appears again at the end of the same verse, so the Chronicles reading may preserve the original. Still others suggest Goliath was a name or title borne by more than one warrior. Some translations, such as the King James Version, harmonize 2 Samuel 21:19 by supplying the words the brother of.

As for Bathsheba, the Chronicler is not hiding it; his readers knew Samuel. He writes selectively throughout, focusing on David as founder of temple worship and bearer of God's promise. He does include David's great sin in the census of chapter 21, told honestly and at length, so his David is not sinless.

questions: Verse 1 notes that David stayed home while the army went to war. Where have moments of idleness or withdrawal been dangerous for you?
The giants of Gath fell to ordinary soldiers, not only to David. What difference does it make that God works through many people rather than one hero?
The Chronicler tells David's story selectively for a purpose. How do you tell your own story, and what does your selection reveal about what you think matters?
